subject: Science
title: Electricity
summary: What electric current is, what pushes it around a circuit, how Ohm's law ties current to potential difference, what decides the resistance of a wire, how resistors add up in series and in parallel, why a current heats a wire, and how electric power and energy are measured and paid for. It is the most numerical chapter in Class 10 Science and the one where a 3- or 5-mark question with a derivation plus a calculation appears almost every year.

exam_profile.weightage: Class 10 Science is one 80-mark paper covering physics, chemistry and biology. Electricity sits in the unit Effects of Current together with Magnetic Effects of Electric Current, and that unit carries about 13 marks. From this chapter alone you can typically expect 6 to 8 marks: an MCQ or assertion-reason item, a 2- or 3-mark numerical, and either a 5-mark derivation-plus-numerical or a case-based passage on a circuit.

question_types.note: Unit of resistivity, what happens to resistance when a wire is stretched or cut, which formula is not power, the reading of an ammeter or voltmeter in a simple circuit, which bulb glows brighter in series, the value of 1 kWh in joules, reading a V–I graph.

Alloys in heating elements, tungsten in filaments, the cord of a heater staying cool while the element glows, current being the same in series, the voltmeter having high resistance, copper for transmission wires.

State Ohm's law and draw the V–I graph; define resistivity with its SI unit; number of electrons in a given charge; what happens to resistance when length or area changes; why series connection is not used at home; what an electric fuse is and what it is made of.

A three-resistor combination numerical (find equivalent resistance, current, potential difference across one resistor, power in one resistor); arranging three equal resistors to get a stated value; Joule's law with a heat calculation; power and energy of a rated appliance; two rated bulbs compared for resistance and current.

Ohm's law with the experimental circuit, the V–I graph and a numerical; derivation of the equivalent resistance in series or in parallel followed by a numerical; heating effect derived from W = VIt with applications and a calculation.
A passage on a household circuit, an electricity bill, the resistivity table, or a V–I graph of two conductors, followed by four sub-parts, at least one of which is a calculation.

hot_topics: Ohm's law: statement, the circuit used to verify it, the V–I graph and its slope, and the definition of 1 ohm
Resistors in series and in parallel: the two derivations and numericals on three-resistor combinations
Factors on which resistance depends: R = ρl/A, resistivity of metals versus alloys, what happens to R when a wire is stretched, cut or doubled in area
Heating effect of current: derivation of H = I<sup>2</sup>Rt, Joule's law in words, and the applications (heater, bulb filament, fuse)
Electric power and energy: P = VI = I<sup>2</sup>R = V<sup>2</sup>/R, rated appliances, the kilowatt hour and the electricity bill

Circuit diagrams: correct symbols, ammeter in series, voltmeter in parallel, polarity of cells
Electric current, charge and potential difference: I = Q/t, V = W/Q, the number of electrons in one coulomb

sections.heading: 11.1 Electric Current and Circuit
sections.body:
An electric circuit is a continuous and closed path along which electric charge can flow. Break the path anywhere, by opening a switch or a plug key, and the current stops. That is all the torch does: the switch closes the path between the cells and the bulb.

Electric current is the rate of flow of electric charge through a cross-section of a conductor. If a net charge Q flows through a cross-section in time t, then I = Q/t. The SI unit of charge is the coulomb (C). One coulomb is the charge carried by about 6 × 1018 electrons, because each electron carries 1.6 × 10−19 C. The SI unit of current is the ampere (A), named after André-Marie Ampère: one ampere is one coulomb of charge flowing per second, 1 A = 1 C/s. Smaller currents are written in milliampere (1 mA = 10−3 A) and microampere (1 μA = 10−6 A).

Two things about direction trip students up. In a metal the charges that actually move are electrons, which are negative. By convention, though, the direction of current is taken as the direction in which positive charge would flow, that is from the positive terminal of the cell, through the circuit, to the negative terminal. So the conventional current is opposite to the direction of electron flow. Say this clearly when asked.

Current is measured with an ammeter. It is always connected in series with the part of the circuit where the current is to be measured, so that the whole current passes through it, and it has a very low resistance so that it does not itself reduce the current. A typical one-mark numerical: a current of 0.5 A flows for 10 minutes; the charge that passes is Q = It = 0.5 × 600 = 300 C, and the number of electrons is 300 ÷ (1.6 × 10−19) = 1.875 × 1021. Convert minutes to seconds before you do anything else.
sections.tip: If a question gives time in minutes or hours, write the conversion to seconds as the first line. Marks are lost more often on 10 min = 600 s than on the formula.

sections.heading: 11.2 Electric Potential and Potential Difference
sections.body:
Charge does not flow through a wire on its own, just as water does not flow through a horizontal pipe unless there is a pressure difference between its ends. In a conductor the electrons need a difference of electric pressure, called the potential difference, to push them along. A cell or a battery maintains this potential difference by the chemical action inside it, and it keeps doing so as long as the chemicals last.

The potential difference between two points in an electric circuit carrying some current is defined as the work done to move a unit charge from one point to the other: V = W/Q. Its SI unit is the volt (V), after Alessandro Volta. One volt is the potential difference between two points when 1 joule of work is done to move a charge of 1 coulomb between them: 1 V = 1 J/C. So a 6 V battery gives 6 J of energy to every coulomb that passes through it, a favourite one-mark question.

The potential difference is measured with a voltmeter. It is always connected in parallel across the two points between which the potential difference is required, and it has a very high resistance so that hardly any current is diverted through it. Contrast this with the ammeter, which goes in series and has low resistance. Students regularly swap these two in circuit diagrams and in one-mark questions, so fix the pair now: ammeter, series, low resistance; voltmeter, parallel, high resistance.

A simple numerical: how much work is done in moving a charge of 2 C across two points having a potential difference of 12 V? W = VQ = 12 × 2 = 24 J. Keep the definition and the unit sentence ready; together they are a standard 2-mark answer.

where: 1 joule of work per coulomb of charge

sections.tip: Write the definition of the volt as a full sentence, with both the joule and the coulomb in it. A bare V = W/Q gets only half the marks for a definition question.

sections.heading: 11.3 Circuit Diagram
sections.body:
A circuit diagram is a drawing of a circuit using conventional symbols instead of pictures of the real components. Examiners expect the NCERT symbols exactly, and a circuit drawn with the wrong symbols or wrong placement of meters can cost a full mark even when the calculation is right.

The symbols you must be able to draw: an electric cell is a long thin line next to a short thick line, the longer line being the positive terminal; a battery is two or more such cells in a row; a plug key or switch is drawn open (a gap with a plug beside it) or closed (the plug in the gap); a wire joint is a dot where the lines meet; wires crossing without joining are drawn as one line hopping over the other with no dot; an electric bulb is a circle with a loop inside it; a resistor of fixed resistance is a small rectangle (or a zigzag); a variable resistance or rheostat is a rectangle with an arrow through it; an ammeter is a circle with the letter A and a positive and negative terminal; a voltmeter is a circle with the letter V and its terminals.

Three placement rules decide the marks. The ammeter is in series so that the entire current passes through it. The voltmeter is in parallel across the component whose potential difference is wanted. The positive terminal of each meter must be connected towards the positive terminal of the cell, otherwise the pointer deflects the wrong way. The plug key is placed in series so that it can break the whole circuit.

When a question says 'draw a circuit diagram to show a battery of three cells of 2 V each, a 5 Ω resistor, an 8 Ω resistor and a 12 Ω resistor in series with a plug key and an ammeter', draw the loop neatly with straight lines and right-angle corners, label every component with its value, and put the ammeter anywhere in the loop, since in series the current is the same everywhere. Then, if asked, note that the ammeter reads 6 V ÷ 25 Ω = 0.24 A.
sections.tip: Draw circuit diagrams with a pencil and a ruler; put arrows for current direction from the positive terminal of the battery; label values on every resistor.

sections.heading: 11.4 Ohm's Law
sections.body:
Ohm's law states that the potential difference V across the ends of a given metallic wire in an electric circuit is directly proportional to the current I flowing through it, provided its temperature remains the same. That is, V ∝ I, or V/I = constant = R, or V = IR. The constant R is the resistance of the conductor. It is a property of the conductor that opposes the flow of charge. Its SI unit is the ohm (Ω): if a potential difference of 1 V across the ends of a conductor makes a current of 1 A flow through it, its resistance is 1 Ω, so 1 Ω = 1 V/1 A. Both the statement of the law and the definition of the ohm carry marks, so write both when asked to state Ohm's law.

The verification is NCERT Activity 11.1 and the board asks for it as a 3- or 5-mark question. Set up a circuit with a nichrome wire XY, an ammeter, a voltmeter across XY, a plug key, and a cell. Take the reading of the ammeter and the voltmeter with one cell, then repeat with two, three and four cells in series. Tabulate V and I. You find that V/I is the same in every row. Plot V on the y-axis against I on the x-axis: the graph is a straight line passing through the origin, and its slope, V/I, gives the resistance of the wire. A steeper line (larger V for the same I) means a larger resistance. The board version often gives you the table or the graph and asks you to find R, or gives two graphs for wires A and B and asks which has more resistance: the steeper one when V is on the y-axis.

Rewriting the law as I = V/R shows why resistance matters: for the same potential difference, doubling the resistance halves the current. A component that gives a large resistance is a resistor; one with a small resistance is a good conductor. A variable resistance, or rheostat, is used in a circuit to change the current without changing the source.

Two conditions belong to the law and examiners look for them: it applies to metallic conductors, and the temperature and other physical conditions must stay constant. The filament of a bulb does not obey it once it heats up, because its resistance rises with temperature.

formulas.expr: R = slope of the V–I graph (V on y-axis, I on x-axis)
where: ΔV/ΔI, a straight line through the origin for a metallic conductor at constant temperature

sections.tip: When you draw the V–I graph, write which quantity is on which axis. If the question puts I on the y-axis, the slope is 1/R and the steeper line has the smaller resistance.

sections.heading: 11.5 Factors on which the Resistance of a Conductor Depends
sections.body:
NCERT Activity 11.2 leads to three results. A longer wire of the same material and thickness gives a smaller current, so resistance is directly proportional to length: R ∝ l. A thicker wire of the same material and length gives a larger current, so resistance is inversely proportional to the area of cross-section: R ∝ 1/A. A wire of a different material with the same length and thickness gives a different current, so resistance depends on the nature of the material. Resistance also depends on temperature (it rises for metals as they get hotter). Combining the first two, R = ρl/A, where ρ (rho) is a constant of proportionality called the electrical resistivity of the material. Its SI unit is Ω m (from ρ = RA/l).

Resistivity depends only on the material and its temperature, not on the length or thickness of the sample; that is the answer to the one-mark question 'on what does the resistivity of a wire depend'. Metals and alloys have very low resistivity, of the order of 10−8 to 10−6 Ω m, and are good conductors. Insulators like rubber and glass have resistivity of the order of 1012 to 1017 Ω m. From the NCERT table, copper is 1.62 × 10−8 Ω m, aluminium 2.63 × 10−8, tungsten 5.20 × 10−8, iron 10.0 × 10−8, mercury 94.0 × 10−8, and the alloy nichrome 100 × 10−8 Ω m, so iron conducts better than mercury.

Two application statements come up every year. The resistivity of an alloy is generally higher than that of its constituent metals, and alloys do not oxidise (burn) readily at high temperature, so alloys such as nichrome are used in electrical heating devices like toasters and electric irons. Copper and aluminium have among the lowest resistivities, so they are used for electrical transmission lines.

The favourite numerical trap is a wire that is stretched or cut. Stretching a wire to double its length halves its area (volume is constant), so R = ρl/A becomes ρ(2l)/(A/2) = 4R. Cutting a wire into n equal parts gives each part R/n; connecting those parts in parallel gives R/n2. If a wire's length is doubled and you want the same resistance, the area must also be doubled.

where: diameter of the wire; convert mm to m before squaring

sections.tip: A wire stretched to n times its length has n<sup>2</sup> times the resistance. A wire cut into n equal parts joined in parallel has R/n<sup>2</sup>. Both come from R = ρl/A; show the one line of working.

sections.heading: 11.6 Resistance of a System of Resistors: 11.6.1 Resistors in Series
sections.body:
Two or more resistors are in series when they are joined end to end so that the same current flows through each of them. NCERT Activity 11.4 shows this: moving the ammeter to different positions in a series circuit does not change its reading. The potential difference across the whole combination, however, is shared: Activity 11.5 shows that the voltmeter reading across the battery equals the sum of the voltmeter readings across the individual resistors.

The derivation the board rewards, step by step. Let three resistors R1, R2 and R3 be connected in series across a battery of potential difference V, and let the current through the circuit be I. In series the current is the same through each resistor. By Ohm's law the potential differences across them are V1 = IR1, V2 = IR2 and V3 = IR3. The total potential difference is the sum: V = V1 + V2 + V3. If the combination is replaced by a single equivalent resistance Rs that draws the same current I from the same battery, then V = IRs. Equating, IRs = IR1 + IR2 + IR3, so Rs = R1 + R2 + R3. The equivalent resistance of resistors in series equals the sum of the individual resistances. It is always greater than the largest individual resistance, and n identical resistors R in series give nR.

Worked example in the NCERT style: a 9 V battery is connected in series with resistors of 0.2 Ω, 0.3 Ω, 0.4 Ω, 0.5 Ω and 12 Ω. Total resistance = 13.4 Ω, so I = 9/13.4 = 0.67 A, and since the current is the same everywhere in series, 0.67 A flows through the 12 Ω resistor too. To find the potential difference across one resistor, multiply that resistor by the common current: across the 12 Ω resistor it is 0.67 × 12 ≈ 8.06 V.

The examiner is looking for four things in the derivation: the labelled circuit diagram, the statement that current is the same, the addition of potential differences, and the final boxed result. Skip any one and a mark goes.

where: equivalent resistance in series; same current through each resistor; V = V<sub>1</sub> + V<sub>2</sub> + V<sub>3</sub>

sections.tip: In a series circuit the potential difference divides in the ratio of the resistances; the biggest resistor gets the biggest share of V.

sections.heading: 11.6.2 Resistors in Parallel
sections.body:
Resistors are in parallel when they are connected between the same two points, so that the potential difference across each of them is the same, while the current from the battery divides among them (NCERT Activity 11.6).

The derivation. Let R1, R2 and R3 be connected in parallel across a potential difference V. Let the currents through them be I1, I2 and I3, and let the total current be I. The total current is the sum of the branch currents: I = I1 + I2 + I3. By Ohm's law, I1 = V/R1, I2 = V/R2, I3 = V/R3. If Rp is the equivalent resistance, then I = V/Rp. Substituting, V/Rp = V/R1 + V/R2 + V/R3, and dividing by V, 1/Rp = 1/R1 + 1/R2 + 1/R3. The reciprocal of the equivalent resistance in parallel is the sum of the reciprocals of the individual resistances. Rp is always less than the smallest resistance in the group. For two resistors, Rp = R1R2/(R1 + R2), and for n identical resistors R in parallel, Rp = R/n.

A typical numerical: 10 Ω, 15 Ω and 5 Ω in parallel. 1/Rp = 1/10 + 1/15 + 1/5 = (3 + 2 + 6)/30 = 11/30, so Rp = 30/11 = 2.73 Ω, smaller than 5 Ω as it must be. Combination questions ask you to get, say, 13.5 Ω and 6 Ω from three 9 Ω resistors: two in parallel (4.5 Ω) in series with the third gives 13.5 Ω; two in series (18 Ω) in parallel with the third gives 18 × 9/27 = 6 Ω.

Why domestic circuits use parallel and not series, a 2- or 3-mark question: in series the current is the same through every appliance, so a bulb and a heater that need very different currents cannot both work properly; if one appliance fails or is switched off, the circuit breaks and all the others stop; and the total resistance is high, so the current is small. In parallel each appliance gets the full supply voltage, can be switched on and off independently, and the total resistance is low.

where: equivalent resistance in parallel; same V across each; I = I<sub>1</sub> + I<sub>2</sub> + I<sub>3</sub>

formulas.expr: R<sub>p</sub> = R<sub>1</sub>R<sub>2</sub>/(R<sub>1</sub> + R<sub>2</sub>) for two resistors
where: product over sum; for n equal resistors R, R<sub>p</sub> = R/n

sections.tip: After finding R<sub>p</sub>, check it is smaller than the smallest resistor. In a 'find the current through the 2 Ω resistor' question, first find the potential difference across that resistor, then divide.

sections.heading: 11.7 Heating Effect of Electric Current
sections.body:
A battery or cell is a source of electrical energy. Its chemical reaction maintains the potential difference that drives the current, and to keep the current going the source must keep spending energy. Part of that energy may do useful work (turn a motor, for instance); the rest is spent in heat that raises the temperature of the appliance. In a purely resistive circuit, one with only resistors connected to a battery, the whole of the source energy is dissipated as heat. This is the heating effect of electric current.

The derivation, which the board asks for directly. Consider a current I flowing through a resistor of resistance R, with potential difference V across it. Let a charge Q flow through it in time t. The work done in moving the charge Q through a potential difference V is W = VQ. Therefore the source supplies energy VQ in time t, and the power input is P = VQ/t = VI. The energy supplied in time t is Pt = VIt. This energy is dissipated in the resistor as heat, so H = VIt. Using Ohm's law V = IR, H = I2Rt. This is Joule's law of heating.

The law in words, three parts, each worth a mark: the heat produced in a resistor is directly proportional to the square of the current for a given resistance, directly proportional to the resistance for a given current, and directly proportional to the time for which the current flows.

Worked example, NCERT Example 11.9 style: an electric iron of resistance 20 Ω takes a current of 5 A. Heat developed in 30 s is H = I2Rt = 52 × 20 × 30 = 25 × 20 × 30 = 15000 J. Choose the form of the formula that uses the quantities given. If V is fixed and R changes, use H = V2t/R; halving R at the same voltage doubles the heat. If I is fixed, use I2Rt.
sections.tip: Joule's law has three proportionalities. Writing only H ∝ I<sup>2</sup> is a one-mark answer to a three-mark question.

sections.heading: 11.7.1 Practical Applications of Heating Effect of Electric Current
sections.body:
The heating of a conductor is often unwanted. It raises the temperature of components and changes their properties, and a lot of the energy in a bulb is lost as heat rather than light. But the same effect is used deliberately in the electric laundry iron, the immersion heater, the toaster, the oven, the kettle and the heater. Their heating elements are made of nichrome, an alloy, for three reasons that examiners like listed: nichrome has a high resistivity so that a short coil gives a lot of heat, a high melting point so that it does not melt at red heat, and it does not oxidise readily at high temperatures.

The electric bulb works on the same effect. The filament must retain as much of the heat as possible so that it gets very hot and emits light, so it must not melt at such high temperatures. Tungsten is used almost exclusively for the filament because it has a very high melting point (3380 °C) and a high resistivity. The bulbs are filled with chemically inactive gases like nitrogen and argon, which prolong the life of the filament by preventing it from oxidising.

The electric fuse is the safety application. It protects circuits and appliances by stopping the flow of any unduly high current. A fuse is a piece of wire made of a metal or an alloy of appropriate melting point, for example aluminium, copper, iron or lead. If a current larger than the specified value flows through the circuit, the fuse wire heats up and melts, which breaks the circuit. The fuse is placed in series with the device, on the live wire. Domestic fuses are rated 1 A, 2 A, 3 A, 5 A, 10 A and so on. To pick the rating, work out the normal current: an electric iron of 1 kW on a 220 V supply draws 1000/220 = 4.5 A, so a 5 A fuse is used.

Why does the heating element of an electric heater glow red while its connecting cord stays cool? Both carry the same current, but the element has a much higher resistance (nichrome, thin, long) than the copper cord, and heat produced is I2Rt, so the element produces far more heat and glows.

formulas.expr: Fuse rating: choose the standard rating just above I = P/V

sections.tip: For 'why tungsten' give two properties (very high melting point of 3380 °C and high resistivity). For 'why nichrome' give three (high resistivity, high melting point, does not oxidise).

sections.heading: 11.8 Electric Power
sections.body:
Electric power is the rate at which electrical energy is consumed or dissipated in a circuit: P = W/t. Since the energy delivered in time t is VIt, P = VI. Using Ohm's law this can be written as P = I2R = V2/R. The SI unit is the watt (W): the power consumed by a device that carries 1 A of current when operated at a potential difference of 1 V, so 1 W = 1 volt × 1 ampere. Practical amounts are given in kilowatt, 1 kW = 1000 W.

Which form to use is the whole art of these numericals. When an appliance is rated, say 100 W at 220 V, the two numbers give you its resistance from R = V2/P = 2202/100 = 484 Ω, and its normal current from I = P/V = 100/220 = 0.45 A. That resistance is a property of the bulb and stays the same if it is put on a different voltage; only the power changes. So a 220 V, 100 W bulb on 110 V gives P = V2/R = 1102/484 = 25 W, a quarter. A 100 W bulb has a lower resistance than a 40 W bulb of the same rating. In parallel on 220 V (the household case) the 100 W bulb draws more current and glows brighter. In series the current is the same through both, so heat produced is I2R and the 40 W bulb, with the higher resistance, glows brighter.

Electrical energy is power multiplied by time: W = Pt. The joule is too small for household use, so the commercial unit is the kilowatt hour: the energy consumed at the rate of 1 kW for 1 hour. 1 kWh = 1000 W × 3600 s = 3.6 × 106 J. This is the 'unit' on your electricity bill. Note carefully: the watt and kilowatt are units of power, the kilowatt hour is a unit of energy; confusing the two is a marked error.

Worked bill example: four 60 W bulbs used for 5 hours a day for 30 days consume 4 × 60 × 5 × 30 = 36000 Wh = 36 kWh. At ₹6 per unit the cost is ₹216.

where: energy used at 1 kW for 1 hour; the commercial unit

sections.tip: From a rating 'P W, V V', first find R = V<sup>2</sup>/P. R stays fixed when the voltage changes; recompute power with P = V<sup>2</sup>/R.

diagrams.title: Circuit to verify Ohm's law (NCERT Activity 11.1)
diagrams.how_to_draw: Draw a rectangular loop with a battery of four cells (long line positive), a plug key, an ammeter (circle with A) and a nichrome wire XY drawn as a resistor, all in series. Connect a voltmeter (circle with V) across the ends X and Y in parallel. Mark the + terminals of both meters towards the + of the battery, and show the current direction with an arrow. Label every component; the labelled voltmeter across XY and the ammeter in the loop are what the marks are for.

diagrams.title: V–I graph for a metallic conductor
diagrams.how_to_draw: Draw axes with I (A) on the x-axis and V (V) on the y-axis, both starting at the origin. Draw a straight line through the origin sloping upward, label it 'V ∝ I', and mark that the slope ΔV/ΔI equals the resistance R. If asked to compare two conductors, draw two lines from the origin and label the steeper one as the higher resistance.

diagrams.title: Three resistors in series with an ammeter and voltmeter
diagrams.how_to_draw: Draw a loop containing a battery, a plug key, an ammeter and three resistors R<sub>1</sub>, R<sub>2</sub>, R<sub>3</sub> drawn one after another along the same wire. Show a voltmeter across the whole combination (or across one resistor if asked). Mark the same current I flowing through every part with arrows, and label V<sub>1</sub>, V<sub>2</sub>, V<sub>3</sub> across the resistors so that V = V<sub>1</sub> + V<sub>2</sub> + V<sub>3</sub> can be quoted from the figure.

diagrams.title: Three resistors in parallel
diagrams.how_to_draw: Draw two vertical junction points joined by three horizontal branches, each carrying one resistor R<sub>1</sub>, R<sub>2</sub>, R<sub>3</sub>. Connect the battery, plug key and an ammeter in the main line outside the junctions. Mark the branch currents I<sub>1</sub>, I<sub>2</sub>, I<sub>3</sub> and the main current I so that I = I<sub>1</sub> + I<sub>2</sub> + I<sub>3</sub>, put dots at the junctions, and show a voltmeter across the two junction points to indicate the common potential difference V.

ncert_questions.q: Calculate the number of electrons constituting one coulomb of charge.
ncert_questions.a: Charge on one electron e = 1.6 × 10−19 C. Number of electrons in 1 C, n = Q/e = 1 ÷ (1.6 × 10−19) = 6.25 × 1018, that is about 6 × 1018 electrons.

ncert_questions.q: How much energy is given to each coulomb of charge passing through a 6 V battery?
ncert_questions.a: Potential difference V = W/Q, so W = VQ = 6 V × 1 C = 6 J. Each coulomb receives 6 joules of energy.

ncert_questions.q: Judge the equivalent resistance when the following are connected in parallel: (a) 1 Ω and 10<sup>6</sup> Ω, (b) 1 Ω, 10<sup>3</sup> Ω and 10<sup>6</sup> Ω.
ncert_questions.a: In a parallel combination the equivalent resistance is always less than the smallest resistance. (a) 1/Rp = 1/1 + 1/106 ≈ 1, so Rp is just under 1 Ω. (b) 1/Rp = 1 + 10−3 + 10−6 ≈ 1.001, so Rp ≈ 0.999 Ω, again just less than 1 Ω. In both cases the large resistors carry almost no current and the answer is approximately 1 Ω.

ncert_questions.q: An electric lamp of 100 Ω, a toaster of 50 Ω and a water filter of 500 Ω are connected in parallel to a 220 V source. What is the resistance of an electric iron connected to the same source that takes as much current as all three appliances, and what is the current through it?
How can three resistors of 2 Ω, 3 Ω and 6 Ω be connected to give a total resistance of (a) 4 Ω, (b) 1 Ω?
ncert_questions.a:
(a) Connect 3 Ω and 6 Ω in parallel: R = 3 × 6/(3 + 6) = 2 Ω. Put this in series with the 2 Ω resistor: 2 + 2 = 4 Ω.

(b) Connect all three in parallel: 1/R = 1/2 + 1/3 + 1/6 = (3 + 2 + 1)/6 = 1, so R = 1 Ω.

ncert_questions.q: What is (a) the highest, (b) the lowest total resistance that can be secured by combinations of four coils of resistance 4 Ω, 8 Ω, 12 Ω, 24 Ω?
ncert_questions.a:
(a) Highest: all four in series, R = 4 + 8 + 12 + 24 = 48 Ω.

(b) Lowest: all four in parallel, 1/R = 1/4 + 1/8 + 1/12 + 1/24 = (6 + 3 + 2 + 1)/24 = 12/24 = 1/2, so R = 2 Ω.

ncert_questions.q: Why does the cord of an electric heater not glow while the heating element does?
ncert_questions.a: The heating element is made of nichrome, an alloy of high resistivity, so its resistance is much higher than that of the copper cord. The same current passes through both, and heat produced is H = I2Rt, so far more heat is produced in the element; it becomes red hot and glows, while the cord, with negligible resistance, stays cool.

ncert_questions.q: An electric motor takes 5 A from a 220 V line. Determine the power of the motor and the energy consumed in 2 h.
ncert_questions.a: Power P = VI = 220 × 5 = 1100 W = 1.1 kW. Energy consumed in 2 h: W = Pt = 1.1 kW × 2 h = 2.2 kWh (= 2.2 × 3.6 × 106 = 7.92 × 106 J).

ncert_questions.q: A piece of wire of resistance R is cut into five equal parts. These parts are then connected in parallel. If the equivalent resistance of this combination is R', then the ratio R/R' is (a) 1/25 (b) 1/5 (c) 5 (d) 25.
ncert_questions.a: (d) 25. Each part has resistance R/5. Five such parts in parallel: 1/R' = 5 × (5/R) = 25/R, so R' = R/25 and R/R' = 25.

ncert_questions.q: An electric bulb is rated 220 V and 100 W. When it is operated on 110 V, the power consumed will be (a) 100 W (b) 75 W (c) 50 W (d) 25 W.
ncert_questions.a: (d) 25 W. Resistance of the bulb R = V2/P = 2202/100 = 484 Ω, which does not change. On 110 V, P = V2/R = 1102/484 = 12100/484 = 25 W. Halving the voltage quarters the power.

ncert_questions.q: Two conducting wires of the same material and of equal lengths and equal diameters are first connected in series and then in parallel in a circuit across the same potential difference. The ratio of heat produced in series and parallel combinations would be (a) 1:2 (b) 2:1 (c) 1:4 (d) 4:1.
ncert_questions.a: (c) 1:4. Let each wire have resistance R. In series Rs = 2R; in parallel Rp = R/2. At the same V for the same time, H = V2t/R, so Hs/Hp = Rp/Rs = (R/2)/(2R) = 1/4.

ncert_questions.q: A copper wire has diameter 0.5 mm and resistivity 1.6 × 10<sup>−8</sup> Ω m. What will be the length of this wire to make its resistance 10 Ω? How much does the resistance change if the diameter is doubled?
ncert_questions.a:
Radius r = 0.25 mm = 2.5 × 10−4 m. Area A = πr2 = 3.14 × (2.5 × 10−4)2 = 3.14 × 6.25 × 10−8 = 1.96 × 10−7 m2.

From R = ρl/A, l = RA/ρ = 10 × 1.96 × 10−7 ÷ (1.6 × 10−8) = 122.7 m (about 122.5 m to 123 m depending on rounding).

If the diameter is doubled, the area becomes four times, and since R ∝ 1/A the resistance becomes one-fourth: 10/4 = 2.5 Ω.

ncert_questions.q: The values of current I flowing in a given resistor for the corresponding values of potential difference V across the resistor are: I (A) = 0.5, 1.0, 2.0, 3.0, 4.0; V (V) = 1.6, 3.4, 6.7, 10.2, 13.2. Plot a graph between V and I and calculate the resistance of that resistor.
ncert_questions.a: Plot I on the x-axis and V on the y-axis; the points lie close to a straight line through the origin, so the resistor obeys Ohm's law. Resistance = slope of the V–I graph. Taking the values V/I: 1.6/0.5 = 3.2, 3.4/1.0 = 3.4, 6.7/2.0 = 3.35, 10.2/3.0 = 3.4, 13.2/4.0 = 3.3. The average is about 3.3 Ω, so R ≈ 3.3 Ω.

ncert_questions.q: When a 12 V battery is connected across an unknown resistor, there is a current of 2.5 mA in the circuit. Find the value of the resistance of the resistor.
How many 176 Ω resistors (in parallel) are required to carry 5 A on a 220 V line?
ncert_questions.a: Required equivalent resistance R = V/I = 220/5 = 44 Ω. For n equal resistors of 176 Ω in parallel, R = 176/n. So 176/n = 44, n = 176/44 = 4. Four resistors are needed.

ncert_questions.q: Show how you would connect three resistors, each of resistance 6 Ω, so that the combination has a resistance of (i) 9 Ω, (ii) 4 Ω.
ncert_questions.a:
(i) Connect two 6 Ω resistors in parallel: 6 × 6/12 = 3 Ω. Connect this in series with the third: 3 + 6 = 9 Ω.

(ii) Connect two 6 Ω resistors in series: 12 Ω. Connect this in parallel with the third: 12 × 6/(12 + 6) = 72/18 = 4 Ω.

Draw both circuit diagrams with the resistors labelled 6 Ω.

ncert_questions.q: Several electric bulbs designed to be used on a 220 V electric supply line are rated 10 W. How many lamps can be connected in parallel with each other across the two wires of the 220 V line if the maximum allowable current is 5 A?
ncert_questions.a:
Current drawn by one bulb I = P/V = 10/220 A = 0.0455 A. Number of bulbs n = 5 ÷ (10/220) = 5 × 220/10 = 110.

Check by resistance: each bulb R = V2/P = 2202/10 = 4840 Ω; for 5 A at 220 V the combination must be 44 Ω; 4840/n = 44 gives n = 110.

ncert_questions.q: A hot plate of an electric oven connected to a 220 V line has two resistance coils A and B, each of 24 Ω resistance, which may be used separately, in series, or in parallel. What are the currents in the three cases?
Compare the power used in the 2 Ω resistor in each of the following circuits: (i) a 6 V battery in series with 1 Ω and 2 Ω resistors, and (ii) a 4 V battery in parallel with 12 Ω and 2 Ω resistors.
ncert_questions.a:
(i) Total resistance = 1 + 2 = 3 Ω; I = 6/3 = 2 A. Power in 2 Ω: P = I2R = 22 × 2 = 8 W.

(ii) In parallel the 2 Ω resistor has the full 4 V across it. P = V2/R = 42/2 = 8 W.

The power used in the 2 Ω resistor is the same in both, 8 W; ratio 1:1.

ncert_questions.q: Two lamps, one rated 100 W at 220 V and the other 60 W at 220 V, are connected in parallel to the electric mains supply. What current is drawn from the line if the supply voltage is 220 V?
ncert_questions.a:
In parallel each lamp gets 220 V and works at its rated power. Total power = 100 + 60 = 160 W. Current drawn I = P/V = 160/220 = 0.727 A (about 0.73 A).

Alternatively, I1 = 100/220 = 0.455 A, I2 = 60/220 = 0.273 A, total 0.727 A.

ncert_questions.q: Which uses more energy, a 250 W TV set in 1 hr, or a 1200 W toaster in 10 minutes?
ncert_questions.a: TV: W = Pt = 250 × 3600 = 9.0 × 105 J. Toaster: W = 1200 × 600 = 7.2 × 105 J. The TV set uses more energy.

ncert_questions.q: An electric heater of resistance 8 Ω draws 15 A from the service mains for 2 hours. Calculate the rate at which heat is developed in the heater.
ncert_questions.a: Rate of heat developed is the power: P = I2R = 152 × 8 = 225 × 8 = 1800 J/s = 1800 W. The 2 hours is not needed for the rate; total heat in 2 h would be 1800 × 7200 = 1.296 × 107 J.

ncert_questions.q: Explain the following. (a) Why is the tungsten used almost exclusively for filament of electric lamps? (b) Why are the conductors of electric heating devices, such as bread-toasters and electric irons, made of an alloy rather than a pure metal? (c) Why is the series arrangement not used for domestic circuits? (d) How does the resistance of a wire vary with its area of cross-section? (e) Why are copper and aluminium wires usually employed for electricity transmission?
ncert_questions.a:
(a) Tungsten has a very high melting point (3380 °C) and high resistivity, so it can be heated to a very high temperature to emit light without melting.

(b) The resistivity of an alloy is higher than that of its constituent metals, so a short coil gives a lot of heat, and alloys do not oxidise or burn readily at high temperature.

(c) In series the same current flows through every appliance, so appliances needing different currents cannot work properly; if one appliance fails the circuit breaks and all stop; appliances cannot be switched on and off independently; and the total resistance is high, so the current is small.

(d) Resistance is inversely proportional to the area of cross-section, R ∝ 1/A (R = ρl/A). Doubling the area halves the resistance.

(e) Copper and aluminium have very low resistivity, so they are good conductors and little energy is lost as heat in the transmission wires.

pyq.q: The maximum resistance which can be made using four resistors each of 2 Ω is
pyq.answer: c
pyq.solution: The maximum resistance from a set of resistors is obtained by connecting all of them in series: 2 + 2 + 2 + 2 = 8 Ω. (The minimum, all in parallel, would be 0.5 Ω.)

pyq.q: The electrical resistivity of a given metallic wire depends upon
pyq.answer: d
pyq.solution: Resistivity is a property of the material (and its temperature) only; length, thickness and shape affect resistance, not resistivity.

pyq.q: Two bulbs rated 100 W; 220 V and 40 W; 220 V are connected in series across a 220 V supply. The ratio of the currents flowing through them is
pyq.answer: c
pyq.solution: In a series circuit the same current flows through every component, so the ratio is 1 : 1. The 40 W bulb, having the higher resistance (1210 Ω against 484 Ω), produces more heat (I<sup>2</sup>R) and glows brighter.

pyq.q: A wire of resistance R is stretched uniformly so that its length becomes double. Its new resistance is
pyq.answer: d
pyq.solution: Volume stays constant, so doubling the length halves the area. R = ρl/A becomes ρ(2l)/(A/2) = 4R.

pyq.q: The SI unit of resistivity is
pyq.answer: b
pyq.solution: From ρ = RA/l, the unit is Ω × m<sup>2</sup> ÷ m = Ω m.

pyq.q: One kilowatt hour is equal to
pyq.answer: c
pyq.solution: 1 kWh = 1000 W × 3600 s = 3.6 × 10<sup>6</sup> J. It is a unit of energy, not power.

pyq.q: In the circuit shown, a 5 Ω resistor and a 10 Ω resistor are connected in series across a 15 V battery. The potential difference across the 10 Ω resistor is
pyq.answer: c
pyq.solution: Total resistance 15 Ω, current 15/15 = 1 A. Across the 10 Ω resistor V = IR = 1 × 10 = 10 V; the 5 Ω resistor gets the remaining 5 V.

pyq.q: Which of the following statements about a voltmeter is correct?
options: It is connected in series and has low resistance
It is connected in parallel and has low resistance
It is connected in series and has high resistance
It is connected in parallel and has high resistance
pyq.answer: d
pyq.solution: A voltmeter is connected in parallel across the two points and must have very high resistance so that it draws almost no current from the circuit.

pyq.q: Assertion (A): Alloys are commonly used in electrical heating devices like electric iron and heater. Reason (R): Resistivity of an alloy is generally higher than that of its constituent metals.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
pyq.answer: a
pyq.solution: Both statements are true. The higher resistivity (together with a high melting point and resistance to oxidation) is exactly why alloys like nichrome are chosen for heating elements, so R explains A.

pyq.q: Assertion (A): In a series circuit the current is the same through each resistor. Reason (R): In a series circuit the potential difference across each resistor is the same.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
pyq.answer: c
pyq.solution: A is true: there is only one path, so the same charge passes every resistor per second. R is false: in series the potential difference divides among the resistors in proportion to their resistances; it is in parallel that V is the same across each.

pyq.q: Assertion (A): The heating element of an electric heater glows red hot but its connecting cord does not. Reason (R): The resistance of the heating element is much higher than that of the cord, so for the same current much more heat (I<sup>2</sup>Rt) is produced in the element.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
pyq.answer: a
pyq.solution: Both are true and R is the reason: the nichrome element has high resistivity and the copper cord has very low resistivity, so Joule heating is concentrated in the element.

pyq.q: Assertion (A): An ammeter is always connected in series in a circuit. Reason (R): An ammeter has a very high resistance.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
pyq.answer: c
pyq.solution: A is true: the whole current must pass through the ammeter. R is false: an ammeter has a very low resistance so that it does not reduce the current it measures.

pyq.q: State Ohm's law. Draw a graph showing the variation of potential difference V with current I for a metallic conductor at constant temperature.
pyq.answer:
Ohm's law: at constant temperature, the potential difference V across the ends of a metallic conductor is directly proportional to the current I flowing through it: V ∝ I, or V = IR, where R is the resistance of the conductor.

Graph: V on the y-axis, I on the x-axis; a straight line passing through the origin. Its slope V/I gives the resistance R.

pyq.q: A conductor of length l and area of cross-section A has resistance R. If its length is doubled, what should be its area of cross-section so that its resistance remains R?
pyq.answer: R = ρl/A. With length 2l and area A', R = ρ(2l)/A'. For the resistance to stay R, ρ(2l)/A' = ρl/A, so A' = 2A. The area of cross-section must be doubled.

pyq.q: Why are alloys used in electrical heating devices rather than pure metals? Give two reasons.
pyq.answer:
(i) The resistivity of an alloy is generally higher than that of its constituent metals, so a short length of alloy wire produces a large amount of heat (H = I2Rt).

(ii) Alloys do not oxidise (burn) readily at high temperatures and have high melting points, so the element lasts long. Example: nichrome in heaters and irons.

pyq.q: A current of 0.5 A is drawn by a filament of an electric bulb for 10 minutes. Find the amount of electric charge that flows through the circuit and the number of electrons that pass through the filament.
pyq.answer:
t = 10 min = 600 s. Q = It = 0.5 × 600 = 300 C.

Number of electrons n = Q/e = 300 ÷ (1.6 × 10−19) = 1.875 × 1021 electrons.

pyq.q: What is an electric fuse? Name the material of which a fuse wire is made and state one characteristic of it.
pyq.answer: An electric fuse is a safety device that protects circuits and appliances by stopping the flow of an unduly high current. It consists of a piece of wire of a metal or alloy of low melting point (for example an alloy of lead and tin, or aluminium, copper, iron), connected in series with the appliance. When the current exceeds the rated value, the fuse wire heats up (I2Rt), melts and breaks the circuit. Characteristic: low melting point and suitable resistance.

pyq.q: Define resistivity of a material. Write its SI unit. On what factors does it depend?
pyq.answer: Resistivity of a material is the resistance of a conductor of that material having unit length and unit area of cross-section: ρ = RA/l. SI unit: ohm metre (Ω m). It depends on the nature of the material and on its temperature; it does not depend on the length or area of the conductor.

pyq.q: Show how you would connect three resistors, each of resistance 9 Ω, so that the combination has a resistance of (i) 13.5 Ω, (ii) 6 Ω. Draw the circuit diagrams.
pyq.answer:
(i) Connect two 9 Ω resistors in parallel: R = 9 × 9/(9 + 9) = 4.5 Ω. Connect the third 9 Ω resistor in series with this pair: 4.5 + 9 = 13.5 Ω.

(ii) Connect two 9 Ω resistors in series: 18 Ω. Connect the third 9 Ω in parallel with this: R = 18 × 9/(18 + 9) = 162/27 = 6 Ω.

Draw each arrangement with a battery and label every resistor 9 Ω; one mark is for each correct diagram and one for the working.

pyq.q: An electric lamp of resistance 20 Ω and a conductor of resistance 4 Ω are connected in series to a 6 V battery. Calculate (a) the total resistance of the circuit, (b) the current through the circuit, (c) the potential difference across the electric lamp and the conductor, and (d) the power of the lamp.
pyq.answer:
(a) Total resistance R = 20 + 4 = 24 Ω.

(b) Current I = V/R = 6/24 = 0.25 A.

(c) Across the lamp: V = IR = 0.25 × 20 = 5 V. Across the conductor: 0.25 × 4 = 1 V. (Check: 5 + 1 = 6 V.)

(d) Power of the lamp P = I2R = 0.252 × 20 = 0.0625 × 20 = 1.25 W (or VI = 5 × 0.25 = 1.25 W).

pyq.q: Derive an expression for the equivalent resistance of three resistors R<sub>1</sub>, R<sub>2</sub> and R<sub>3</sub> connected in parallel.
pyq.answer:
Draw R1, R2, R3 connected between the same two points across a battery of potential difference V. In parallel the potential difference across each resistor is the same, V, and the main current I divides into I1, I2, I3, so I = I1 + I2 + I3.

By Ohm's law, I1 = V/R1, I2 = V/R2, I3 = V/R3. If Rp is the equivalent resistance, I = V/Rp.

Hence V/Rp = V/R1 + V/R2 + V/R3, and dividing by V: 1/Rp = 1/R1 + 1/R2 + 1/R3. The equivalent resistance is less than the smallest of the three.

pyq.q: Two bulbs are rated 40 W; 220 V and 25 W; 220 V. (a) Which bulb has the higher resistance? (b) Which draws more current when connected to a 220 V supply? Support your answer with calculations.
pyq.answer:
Resistance R = V2/P. For the 40 W bulb: 2202/40 = 48400/40 = 1210 Ω. For the 25 W bulb: 48400/25 = 1936 Ω.

(a) The 25 W bulb has the higher resistance (1936 Ω).

(b) Current I = P/V. 40 W bulb: 40/220 = 0.18 A; 25 W bulb: 25/220 = 0.11 A. The 40 W bulb draws more current, so it glows brighter when each is connected separately (or in parallel) to 220 V.

pyq.q: State Joule's law of heating. A charge of 96000 C flows through a conductor for 2 hours when a potential difference of 40 V is applied across it. Calculate the heat produced.
pyq.answer:
Joule's law of heating: the heat produced in a resistor is (i) directly proportional to the square of the current for a given resistance, (ii) directly proportional to the resistance for a given current, and (iii) directly proportional to the time for which the current flows: H = I2Rt.

Numerical: H = VIt = VQ (since Q = It). H = 40 × 96000 = 3.84 × 106 J. (The 2 hours is already included in the charge; if you prefer, I = 96000/7200 = 13.33 A and H = 40 × 13.33 × 7200 = 3.84 × 106 J.)

pyq.q: An electric iron is rated 750 W at 200 V. Calculate (a) the current flowing through it, (b) its resistance, and (c) the energy consumed in 2 hours in kWh and in joules.

(a) State Ohm's law. (b) Draw a labelled circuit diagram of the arrangement used to verify it in the laboratory and describe the procedure briefly. (c) Draw the V–I graph obtained and state what its slope gives. (d) Define one ohm.
pyq.answer:
(a) Ohm's law: the potential difference V across the ends of a metallic conductor is directly proportional to the current I flowing through it, provided its temperature remains constant. V ∝ I, V = IR.

(b) Circuit: a nichrome wire XY, an ammeter and a plug key connected in series with one cell; a voltmeter connected in parallel across XY. Procedure: close the key and note the ammeter reading I and the voltmeter reading V. Repeat with two, three and four cells in series. Tabulate V and I and find V/I for each set of readings. V/I is found to be the same in every case, which verifies the law.

(c) Plot V (y-axis) against I (x-axis): a straight line through the origin. The slope V/I of the line gives the resistance R of the wire.

(d) One ohm is the resistance of a conductor through which a current of 1 ampere flows when a potential difference of 1 volt is applied across its ends: 1 Ω = 1 V/1 A.

pyq.q: (a) Three resistors R<sub>1</sub>, R<sub>2</sub> and R<sub>3</sub> are connected in series. Derive the expression for the equivalent resistance of the combination. (b) Show how four resistors, each of 8 Ω, can be connected to give an effective resistance of 8 Ω.
pyq.answer:
(a) Draw R1, R2, R3 end to end across a battery of potential difference V with a current I. In series the same current I flows through each resistor. By Ohm's law the potential differences across them are V1 = IR1, V2 = IR2, V3 = IR3. The total potential difference is V = V1 + V2 + V3. If Rs is the equivalent resistance, V = IRs. So IRs = IR1 + IR2 + IR3, giving Rs = R1 + R2 + R3.

(b) Connect two 8 Ω resistors in series (16 Ω) and the other two in series (16 Ω); then connect the two 16 Ω branches in parallel: 16 × 16/32 = 8 Ω. Alternatively, connect two 8 Ω in parallel (4 Ω) and the other two in parallel (4 Ω), and put the two 4 Ω groups in series: 4 + 4 = 8 Ω. Draw the circuit for the arrangement you choose.

pyq.q: (a) Derive the expression for the heat produced when a current I flows through a resistor R for time t. (b) An electric heater is rated 1000 W at 220 V. Calculate its resistance, the current it draws, and the heat produced in 10 minutes. (c) State two practical applications of the heating effect of electric current.
pyq.answer:
(a) Let a charge Q flow through a resistor R in time t under a potential difference V, so the current is I = Q/t. Work done in moving charge Q through potential difference V is W = VQ. The source therefore supplies energy VQ in time t, and power P = VQ/t = VI. Energy supplied in time t = VIt. In a purely resistive circuit this energy is dissipated entirely as heat, so H = VIt. Substituting V = IR, H = I2Rt. This is Joule's law of heating.

(b) Resistance R = V2/P = 2202/1000 = 48400/1000 = 48.4 Ω. Current I = P/V = 1000/220 = 4.55 A. Heat in 10 min = Pt = 1000 × 600 = 6 × 105 J (check: I2Rt = 4.552 × 48.4 × 600 ≈ 6 × 105 J).

(c) Applications: the electric heater, iron, toaster and kettle, whose nichrome elements produce heat; the electric bulb, whose tungsten filament is heated until it glows; the electric fuse, which melts and breaks the circuit when too large a current flows.

pyq.q:
In a house, all the appliances are connected in parallel across the 220 V mains. A 5 A fuse is placed in series in the live wire. On one evening the family switches on four 60 W bulbs, a 500 W television and a 1000 W electric iron at the same time. The electricity board charges ₹6 per unit, and one unit is one kilowatt hour.
(i) Why are the appliances connected in parallel and not in series?
(ii) Calculate the total current drawn from the mains when all the appliances are on. Will the 5 A fuse blow?
(iii) How much energy in kWh is consumed if the four bulbs alone are used for 5 hours a day for 30 days, and what does it cost?
(iv) State what a fuse is made of and why.
pyq.answer:
(i) In parallel each appliance gets the full 220 V and works at its rated power, can be switched on or off independently, and the failure of one does not stop the others. In series the same current would flow through all, they could not be operated independently, and one failure would break the whole circuit.

(ii) Total power = 4 × 60 + 500 + 1000 = 1740 W. Current I = P/V = 1740/220 = 7.9 A. This exceeds 5 A, so the fuse will melt and break the circuit.

(iii) Energy = 4 × 60 W × 5 h × 30 = 36000 Wh = 36 kWh. Cost = 36 × ₹6 = ₹216.

(iv) A fuse wire is made of a metal or alloy of low melting point (an alloy of lead and tin, or aluminium, copper, iron). When the current exceeds the rated value the wire heats up (I2Rt), melts, and breaks the circuit, protecting the appliances.

pyq.q:
The resistivity of a material is the resistance of a conductor of that material of unit length and unit area of cross-section. From the NCERT table: copper 1.62 × 10−8 Ω m, aluminium 2.63 × 10−8 Ω m, tungsten 5.20 × 10−8 Ω m, iron 10.0 × 10−8 Ω m, nichrome 100 × 10−8 Ω m, glass about 1012 to 1017 Ω m. A student has two wires, one of copper and one of nichrome, each 1 m long with area of cross-section 1 × 10−6 m2.
(i) Calculate the resistance of each wire.
(ii) Which of the two would you use as the heating element of a room heater and why?
(iii) Which material from the table is best for transmission wires and why is glass not used at all?
(iv) If the nichrome wire is stretched to double its length, what will its new resistance be?
pyq.answer:
(i) R = ρl/A. Copper: 1.62 × 10−8 × 1 ÷ 10−6 = 1.62 × 10−2 Ω = 0.0162 Ω. Nichrome: 100 × 10−8 × 1 ÷ 10−6 = 1 Ω.

(ii) Nichrome, because its resistivity is about 60 times that of copper, so a short coil gives a large heat output (H = I2Rt); it also has a high melting point and does not oxidise easily at red heat.

(iii) Copper (with aluminium a close second) because its resistivity is the lowest, so energy loss as heat in the wires is least. Glass is an insulator with resistivity about 1020 times higher than that of metals; it does not conduct current.

(iv) Stretching to double length halves the area (volume constant), so R becomes 4 times: 4 × 1 = 4 Ω.

practice_mcq.q: A current of 2 A flows through a conductor for 5 minutes. The charge that passes through it is
practice_mcq.explanation: Q = It = 2 × (5 × 60) = 600 C. Convert minutes to seconds first.

practice_mcq.q: The correct way to connect an ammeter and a voltmeter in a circuit is
options: ammeter in parallel, voltmeter in series
ammeter in series, voltmeter in parallel
practice_mcq.explanation: The ammeter must carry the whole current (series, low resistance); the voltmeter measures the potential difference across a component (parallel, high resistance).

practice_mcq.q: Three resistors of 6 Ω each are connected in parallel. The equivalent resistance is
practice_mcq.explanation: For n equal resistors in parallel R<sub>p</sub> = R/n = 6/3 = 2 Ω.

practice_mcq.q: A bulb rated 100 W at 250 V has a resistance of
Which of the following is NOT a correct expression for electric power?
practice_mcq.explanation: P = VI = I<sup>2</sup>R = V<sup>2</sup>/R. IR<sup>2</sup> has units of V·Ω, not watts.

practice_mcq.q: The heating element of an electric heater is made of nichrome because nichrome
options: has low resistivity and low melting point
has high resistivity and high melting point
is a good conductor of heat
practice_mcq.explanation: High resistivity means a short coil gives a lot of heat; high melting point and resistance to oxidation mean it survives red heat.

practice_mcq.q: The resistivity of copper is of the order of
practice_mcq.explanation: Copper has resistivity 1.62 × 10<sup>−8</sup> Ω m; metals lie between 10<sup>−8</sup> and 10<sup>−6</sup> Ω m, insulators between 10<sup>12</sup> and 10<sup>17</sup> Ω m.

practice_mcq.q: Resistors of 4 Ω and 12 Ω are connected in parallel. The equivalent resistance is
practice_mcq.explanation: R<sub>p</sub> = 4 × 12/(4 + 12) = 48/16 = 3 Ω, which is less than the smaller resistor, as it should be.

practice_mcq.q: A wire of resistance 8 Ω is cut into two equal halves and the halves are connected in parallel. The resistance of the combination is
practice_mcq.explanation: Each half is 4 Ω; two 4 Ω resistors in parallel give 4/2 = 2 Ω (R/n<sup>2</sup> with n = 2).

practice_mcq.q: Two heaters rated 500 W; 220 V and 1000 W; 220 V are compared. Which has the greater resistance?
practice_mcq.explanation: R = V<sup>2</sup>/P, so at the same rated voltage the lower-power appliance has the higher resistance: 96.8 Ω against 48.4 Ω.

practice_mcq.q: A 60 W bulb is used for 10 hours a day. The energy it consumes in one day is
A potential difference of 1 volt between two points means that
options: 1 C of charge flows per second
1 J of work is done in moving 1 C of charge between them
1 A of current flows between them
the resistance between them is 1 Ω
practice_mcq.explanation: V = W/Q; 1 V = 1 J/C. The first option describes the ampere.

practice_mcq.q: In a V–I graph with V on the y-axis, conductor A gives a steeper line than conductor B. Then
options: A does not obey Ohm's law
practice_mcq.explanation: The slope of the V–I line is V/I = R, so the steeper line belongs to the conductor with more resistance.

practice_mcq.q: An electric fuse should be connected
options: in parallel with the appliance, on the neutral wire
in series with the appliance, on the live wire
practice_mcq.explanation: Only in series does the full current pass through the fuse so that it can melt and break the circuit; it goes on the live wire so that the appliance is disconnected from the high potential.

practice_mcq.q: The direction of conventional current in a metal wire is
options: the same as the direction of electron flow
opposite to the direction of electron flow
practice_mcq.explanation: Conventional current is taken as the direction of flow of positive charge, from the positive to the negative terminal, opposite to the electrons.

practice_mcq.q: A 5 Ω resistor and a 10 Ω resistor are connected in series to a battery. If the current in the circuit is 0.4 A, the potential difference of the battery is
practice_mcq.explanation: Total resistance 15 Ω; V = IR = 0.4 × 15 = 6 V.

common_mistakes: Connecting the ammeter in parallel or the voltmeter in series in a circuit diagram, or drawing the cell with the short thick line as positive. Each costs a mark and the examiner does not read further into that diagram.
Forgetting to convert minutes and hours to seconds, or mA to A, before using I = Q/t or H = I<sup>2</sup>Rt. The formula is right, the number is wrong, and only the formula mark survives.

Writing the parallel formula as R<sub>p</sub> = 1/R<sub>1</sub> + 1/R<sub>2</sub> and stopping there, without taking the reciprocal. Check the answer: R<sub>p</sub> must be smaller than the smallest resistor.

Assuming the resistance of a rated bulb changes when the supply voltage changes. R = V<sup>2</sup>/P from the rating is fixed; only the power consumed changes, so a 220 V, 100 W bulb on 110 V gives 25 W.
Stating Ohm's law without the condition 'provided the temperature remains constant', and stating Joule's law with only one of its three proportionalities.
Saying resistivity depends on the length or thickness of the wire. Resistivity depends only on the material and the temperature; resistance depends on length and area.
Treating the kilowatt hour as a unit of power, or the watt as a unit of energy. kWh is energy (1 kWh = 3.6 × 10<sup>6</sup> J); W and kW are power.

Concluding that the higher-wattage bulb always glows brighter. In series the same current flows, so the bulb with more resistance (lower rated power) glows brighter; in parallel the higher-wattage bulb glows brighter.
strategy:
Divide the chapter into three blocks and give each a sitting. Block one is the definitions: current, coulomb, potential difference, volt, ohm, resistivity, kilowatt hour. Write each as a full sentence with its unit; these are the one- and two-mark questions and they should take you no time in the exam. Block two is the four derivations the board asks for: Ohm's law with the circuit and the V–I graph, series equivalent resistance, parallel equivalent resistance, and H = I2Rt from W = VQ. Write each one out from memory, with the labelled diagram, until you can do all four in fifteen minutes. Block three is numericals. Do every NCERT in-text and exercise problem, then the rated-appliance set (R = V2/P, I = P/V, energy in kWh) and the three-equal-resistor arrangement set (9 Ω to 13.5 Ω and 6 Ω; 6 Ω to 9 Ω and 4 Ω; four 8 Ω to 8 Ω).

In the exam, for any circuit numerical, draw the circuit, reduce the resistors step by step writing each intermediate value, find the total current, and only then find the quantity asked. For a series circuit the current is shared and V divides; for parallel V is shared and current divides. State which case you are in. Give every answer a unit. For 5-mark questions, split your time: about three minutes for the derivation with diagram, three minutes for the numerical, and a minute to check that Rp is smaller than the smallest resistor and that the sum of potential differences equals the battery voltage.

Memorise the resistivity order (copper, aluminium, tungsten, iron, mercury, nichrome), the reasons for tungsten, nichrome and the fuse wire, and the disadvantages of series wiring. Those five short lists cover most of the theory marks.
revision_checklist: I can define current, charge, potential difference and their units, and state 1 C ≈ 6 × 10<sup>18</sup> electrons and 1 V = 1 J/C.
I know conventional current runs from + to − through the circuit, opposite to electron flow.
I can draw all the NCERT circuit symbols, and I put the ammeter in series and the voltmeter in parallel with correct polarity.
I can state Ohm's law with the temperature condition, define 1 ohm, and draw the V–I graph with the slope labelled as R.
I can describe the Ohm's law verification circuit and procedure with a labelled diagram.
I can write R = ρl/A, give the unit of resistivity, and explain what happens to R when a wire is stretched, cut, or doubled in area.
I know the order of resistivities (copper, aluminium, tungsten, iron, mercury, nichrome) and why alloys are used in heaters and copper in transmission wires.
I can derive R<sub>s</sub> = R<sub>1</sub> + R<sub>2</sub> + R<sub>3</sub> with the diagram and the 'same current, V divides' step.
I can derive 1/R<sub>p</sub> = 1/R<sub>1</sub> + 1/R<sub>2</sub> + 1/R<sub>3</sub> with the diagram and the 'same V, current divides' step, and I check R<sub>p</sub> is the smallest.
I can arrange three equal resistors to give the standard target values, and four 8 Ω resistors to give 8 Ω.
I can list four disadvantages of series wiring and the advantages of parallel wiring at home.
I can derive H = I<sup>2</sup>Rt from W = VQ and state Joule's law with all three proportionalities.
I can explain tungsten filaments, inert gas in bulbs, nichrome elements, and the fuse (material, placement, rating).
I can use P = VI = I<sup>2</sup>R = V<sup>2</sup>/R, get R and I from an appliance rating, and recompute power on a different voltage.
I know 1 kWh = 3.6 × 10<sup>6</sup> J is energy, not power, and I can work out an electricity bill.
